findings.title: Cutover step 6 names the WAL to verify via `pg_walfile_name(pg_switch_wal())`, a novel/unchecked expression with no test coverage
findings.description:
`step_switch` (TD8 step 6 / success-criterion 6) does:
```python
segment = psql(TICK, "SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_switch_wal())")
target = ctx.tick.backup_root / "wal" / f"{segment}.zst"
```
The correctness of the whole archiving-verification step hinges on what `pg_switch_wal()` returns. PostgreSQL's `pg_switch_wal()` returns an LSN at/near the segment boundary, and `pg_walfile_name(lsn)` maps an LSN to the segment *containing* it. Whether that is the segment that was just completed (and therefore just archived to `<segment>.zst`) or the newly-opened segment (which is the *current*, not-yet-archived segment) is the crux. If it names the newly-opened segment, then on a freshly provisioned, idle tick cluster that segment's `.zst` will not appear within `WAL_SWITCH_WAIT_S` (120 s), because an open segment is only archived at the *next* switch — so step 6 would time out and fail the cutover even when archiving works perfectly.

Two reinforcing facts:
1. **It is not the method the repo already proves.** Every prior record of this exact operation identifies the archived segment by observation / `pg_stat_archiver.last_archived_wal`, not by `pg_walfile_name(pg_switch_wal())`: runbook 200 ("`pg_switch_wal()` at 13:23: `…1244…F2.zst` landed within 6 s … `last_archived_wal` advanced"), runbook 210, and slice 915's task ("pg_switch_wal() → `last_archived_wal` 00000001000011A600000058"). The cutover introduces a new naming path that has not been validated anywhere in the repo.
2. **No test covers the SQL expression.** `test_wal_wait_gives_up_at_the_bound` and the `step_switch`-adjacent tests stub `psql` to return a fixed name, so an off-by-one in the segment expression is invisible to the suite — only the wait/bound logic is exercised.

I could not run `psql` in this environment, so I'm flagging the ambiguity rather than asserting the direction of the error. Recommended before the PM runs the cutover: empirically confirm on the (idle) tick cluster which `.zst` actually appears after `SELECT pg_switch_wal();` and whether `pg_walfile_name(pg_switch_wal())` equals it; or switch the target to the proven method (capture `last_archived_wal` before and after, and wait for that segment's `.zst`). If the expression does name the open segment, this is a blocking defect for step 6.

findings.title: Redundant `assert` immediately after a `require()` guard
findings.description: In `run_health`, `require(flags is not None, ...)` already raises `StepFailed` when the summary is absent, so the following `assert flags is not None` is unreachable as a real guard and the `assert` is disabled under `python -O` anyway. `block_commands` in `cutover_227_helpers.py` similarly uses `assert match is not None` on a condition that the `_job_lines` filter already guarantees. These are harmless invariants, but the project convention is explicit `StepFailed`/`require` for "saw something unexpected" paths; the extra `assert`s add noise and no behavior. Consider dropping them or keeping only one.

findings.title: `conf_sums()` uses `next(...)` with no default; a StopIteration would bypass the report writer
findings.description: `conf_sums()` does `next(r.split()[5] for r in rows if r.split()[:2] == MAIN.split("/"))`. If the `17/main` row were ever absent from `pg_lsclusters`, this raises `StopIteration` from `step_guards` (the first step). `run_steps` only catches `StepFailed` and `subprocess.CalledProcessError`, so a `StopIteration` would propagate out of `main()` and skip writing the cutover report — violating the "the report is still written on first failure" contract stated in the module docstring. This is a very unlikely path in practice (production always has `17/main`), and `int(psql(...))` in `tick_locks_held` has an analogous (even less likely) `ValueError` risk on empty output. Consider letting these route through `require`/`StepFailed` so the failure is recorded and the report is always emitted.
